response.generated_text:
### G1-2 – Management of relationships with suppliers

Nestlé’s supplier-management approach is grounded in the Nestlé Responsible Sourcing Standard. The Standard communicates basic mandatory requirements and important and urgent sustainability practices to the more than 150 000 direct suppliers and more than 500 000 farmers with whom we work. It covers human rights, environmental matters and, where applicable, animal welfare, including expectations relating to water use and water-resource management.

Our responsible sourcing methodology seeks to establish traceability to the point of origin, defined as the farm or group of farms. Human rights and environmental due diligence systems are used to assess, address and report potential or actual supply-chain impacts. Under this approach, tier-1 suppliers are expected to demonstrate measurable progress in addressing identified impacts in their supply chains and animal-welfare issues where applicable.

Supplier engagement is a core component of remediation. Where assessments identify gaps, we work with suppliers and partners to develop time-bound action plans. Support may extend across suppliers, mills, plantations and smallholders and includes targeted interventions addressing risks such as forced labour and child labour. In the palm oil supply chain, Nestlé has also worked with Verité to assess its global labour-rights management systems and to conduct in-depth supplier reviews examining how the Responsible Sourcing Standard translates into practice throughout the supply chain. We additionally engage through multistakeholder platforms, including the Consumer Goods Forum Forest Positive Coalition, to advocate for regulations, policies, programmes and incentives supportive of labour rights.

Supplier-related risks form part of the Nestlé Group Enterprise Risk Management framework. Annual top-down Group assessments and parallel bottom-up market assessments identify and aggregate key risks, allocate ownership and support mitigating action. Line management is responsible for risk assessments and the resulting mitigation measures. Human rights risks considered include failure to identify or prevent forced labour, child labour, excessive working hours and unfair wages in direct operations and the supply chain. Mitigations include due diligence, responsible sourcing programmes, policies and controls, grievance mechanisms and consequence management. At Board level, the Nomination and Sustainability Committee oversees environmental, social and governance performance and reviews related commitments and reporting.

Consequences may affect commercial relationships. In 2022, 11 contracts with business partners were terminated or not renewed following confirmed corruption- or bribery-related violations, compared with six in 2021.

Our development priority remains moving beyond individual site assessments toward a more comprehensive and systematic approach to assessing, addressing and reporting social, environmental and animal-welfare risks. No specific quantitative supplier-payment-practice target or metric is reported in the available information for 2022.

### G1-2 – Management of relationships with suppliers

Nestlé’s supplier-management approach is grounded in the Nestlé Responsible Sourcing Standard. The Standard communicates basic mandatory requirements and important and urgent sustainability practices to the more than 150 000 direct suppliers and more than 500 000 farmers with whom we work. It covers human rights, environmental matters and, where applicable, animal welfare, including expectations relating to water use and water-resource management.

Our responsible sourcing methodology seeks to establish traceability to the point of origin, defined as the farm or group of farms. Human rights and environmental due diligence systems are used to assess, address and report potential or actual supply-chain impacts. Under this approach, tier-1 suppliers are expected to demonstrate measurable progress in addressing identified impacts in their supply chains and animal-welfare issues where applicable.

Supplier engagement is a core component of remediation. Where assessments identify gaps, we work with suppliers and partners to develop time-bound action plans. Support may extend across suppliers, mills, plantations and smallholders and includes targeted interventions addressing risks such as forced labour and child labour. In the palm oil supply chain, Nestlé has also worked with Verité to assess its global labour-rights management systems and to conduct in-depth supplier reviews examining how the Responsible Sourcing Standard translates into practice throughout the supply chain. We additionally engage through multistakeholder platforms, including the Consumer Goods Forum Forest Positive Coalition, to advocate for regulations, policies, programmes and incentives supportive of labour rights.

Supplier-related risks form part of the Nestlé Group Enterprise Risk Management framework. Annual top-down Group assessments and parallel bottom-up market assessments identify and aggregate key risks, allocate ownership and support mitigating action. Line management is responsible for risk assessments and the resulting mitigation measures. Human rights risks considered include failure to identify or prevent forced labour, child labour, excessive working hours and unfair wages in direct operations and the supply chain. Mitigations include due diligence, responsible sourcing programmes, policies and controls, grievance mechanisms and consequence management. At Board level, the Nomination and Sustainability Committee oversees environmental, social and governance performance and reviews related commitments and reporting.

Consequences may affect commercial relationships. In 2022, 11 contracts with business partners were terminated or not renewed following confirmed corruption- or bribery-related violations, compared with six in 2021.

Our development priority remains moving beyond individual site assessments toward a more comprehensive and systematic approach to assessing, addressing and reporting social, environmental and animal-welfare risks. No specific quantitative supplier-payment-practice target or metric is reported in the available information for 2022.
